newsitem.title: CANADA: Powerful nations push for land mine ban.
newsitem.headline: Powerful nations push for land mine ban.

text.p: Seventy countries launched a conference (on) Thursday aimed at a global ban on anti-personnel land mines, the deadly weapons that blow up farmers and their children long after wars have ceased.

"I am confident that this occasion will provide an important impetus to the global endeavor aimed at putting an end to the scourge of land mines," U.N. Undersecretary-General Yasushi Akashi said at the opening of the three days of talks.

About 500 people -- mostly civilians and many of them children -- are killed or maimed each week by anti-personnel mines, experts estimate. More than 110 million of the mines lurk under the soil in 70 countries.
The meeting itself will not negotiate a ban but the Canadian organizers said they hoped to win agreement to work toward negotiations, perhaps as early as next year.

"We want to ensure...that the ban is real and that it is imminent," said Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, who expressed delight that many more countries were attending than originally expected.
Axworthy said ideally the meeting would push for a ban by 2000.

Forty-seven of the nations -- including the United States, Britain, France, Japan and Germany -- signaled their agreement to push for a total ban by being full participants in the conference, a Canadian official said.

The U.S. representative, Thomas McNamara, said his government supported starting negotiations for a ban as soon as possible, but that more countries would have to join the movement before any such negotiations succeeded.
"A global ban as soon as possible will not occur immediately, but we have to work towards including more countries," McNamara, assistant secretary for political and military affairs, told Reuters.
On Wednesday, France announced its decision to renounce the use of anti-personnel mines, except in extreme cases.
Twenty-four countries were attending as observers, including Russia, Iran, Israel and Egypt.

Russian representative Viatcheslav Sergueev, said his country -- responsible under the Soviet Union for numerous deaths from mines in Afghanistan -- did not support an immediate ban but wanted to see how the idea was advancing.
"The idea of a total ban is a rather new one, and we are here to see how those countries which support it are moving forward," he told Reuters.
China absent, as were most Middle Eastern nations, including Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Libya.
But the former Yugoslavia was well-represented, with Bosnia, Croatia and Slovenia as full participants and Yugoslavia attending as an observer.
Axworthy told Reuters that it would be important eventually to get China on board.

Chris Moon of the private group International Campaign to Ban Landmines said he was encouraged by the fact that nearly 20 nations that had not previously supported an immediate and comprehensive ban were attending the Ottawa conference as full participants.

"The success of this meeting could well determine whether we achieve a ban in the near term -- by the year 2000 or even sooner -- or whether it is accomplished in the long run, one or two decades from now," Moon told the opening session.
